n: First of four short lessons: don’t rashly co-sign for someone else’s debt. Shaking hands was how such a pledge was made.

f.g: surety = one who guarantees another’s debt, like a co-signer.
Struck hands—a handshake that sealed a binding agreement.

n: Your own words have trapped you. A rash promise can catch you like a snare.

f.g: snared = caught in a trap.

n: The fix is urgent humility: go to the person, swallow your pride, and plead to be released from the pledge.

f.g: Press your friend hard; keep pleading with him.

n: Don’t sleep until you have resolved it—this is serious and needs immediate action.

f.w: Give not sleep to thine eyes

n: Escape like a gazelle from a hunter or a bird from a trapper—with all your energy.

f.g: roe = gazelle.
fowler = a bird-catcher.

n: Second lesson: laziness. The lazy person is told to learn from the tiny ant.

f.g: sluggard = a lazy person, a habitual idler.

n: The ant has no boss watching her, yet she works anyway. Self-motivation is part of wisdom.
She stores food in summer and harvest time, preparing for winter. Planning ahead is wise.

f.g: meat = food in general.

f.w: gathereth her food in the harvest

n: The father mockingly asks the sluggard how long he plans to lie there.
The sluggard’s excuse, quoted: just a little more sleep. Small delays add up.

f.w: a little folding of the hands

n: Poverty will arrive like a traveling robber or an armed raider—suddenly and unstoppably.

f.g: Like a vagabond or highwayman who comes unannounced.
want = need, lack.

n: Third lesson: the troublemaker. He is worthless and wicked, going about with crooked talk.

f.g: Hebrew “man of belial”—a worthless, good-for-nothing person (much stronger than modern “naughty”).

n: He communicates with secret signals—winks, foot movements, finger gestures—to deceive or conspire.
His heart is full of perversity; he is always scheming harm and stirring up conflict.
His disaster will come in an instant, and he will be shattered beyond repair.

f.g: Without healing; beyond fixing.

n: Fourth lesson: a list of what the Lord hates. “Six… yea, seven” is a Hebrew number pattern that builds to a climax on the last item.

f.g: The “x, x+1” pattern draws attention to the final item in the list.

n: Arrogant eyes, a lying tongue, and murderous hands. The list moves through parts of the body, showing how sin can take over the whole person.
A heart that plots evil and feet that hurry to do harm—sin starts inside and then moves into action.
A false witness and one who stirs up strife among family or community. The seventh item—sowing discord—is the climax: God especially hates breaking apart people who should be united.
The father returns to his main theme: keep your parents’ teachings.

f.w: forsake not the law of thy mother

n: Keep these teachings always close, bound on your heart and around your neck. The language echoes the command to bind God’s word on hand and forehead.

f.w: Bind them continually upon thine heart

n: These teachings act like a guide in the daytime, a guard at night, and a counselor in the morning—with you at every moment.
God’s commandment is a lamp and his teaching is light; even correction is a road to life.
These lessons especially protect against the smooth talk of the immoral woman.
Don’t let desire for her beauty grow in your heart, or let her capture you with fluttering eyes. Jesus taught the same: sin begins with the heart and eyes.

f.w: Lust not after her beauty in thine heart

n: A prostitute may cost a man his last loaf of bread, but an adulteress hunts his very life. The second is far more dangerous.

f.g: Reduced to poverty, down to a crust.
The very life or soul of a person.

n: A vivid question: can you carry fire against your chest without your clothes catching? Some actions carry unavoidable consequences.

f.g: bosom = chest, the fold of a garment over the chest.

n: Or walk on hot coals without burning your feet? Of course not.
Likewise, the man who sleeps with his neighbor’s wife cannot escape guilt or punishment.

f.g: Will not go unpunished.

n: People may feel some sympathy for a thief who steals because he is starving.

f.g: soul = appetite, life; to satisfy his hunger.

n: Even so, he must repay heavily—possibly everything he owns. Theft has a price that can be paid back.

f.g: “Sevenfold” means full, complete repayment.

n: Adultery is worse: it shows a lack of sense and destroys one’s own soul. Unlike stolen goods, the damage cannot simply be repaid.

f.g: Literally “lacks heart”—has no sense.

n: He will be wounded and disgraced, and the shame will be very hard to erase.

f.g: reproach = disgrace, public shame.

n: A betrayed husband’s jealousy burns like fury; he will show no mercy when he seeks justice.

f.w: jealousy is the rage of a man

n: No payment or gifts will satisfy him. Unlike theft, adultery cannot be bought off.

f.g: ransom = a payment to settle a wrong or buy release.
